extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, trial counsel, and appellate attorneys (Federal Circuit/Third Circuit practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for litigating and appealing post-trial motions in patent infringement cases, including standards for new trials, JMOL (Rule 50) preservation, exclusion of evidence under Rule 403, and claim-construction practices at trial. Focused on Federal Circuit review (applying regional-circuit law where required).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for granting a new trial (Third Circuit)
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court should grant a new trial only if the jury’s verdict is against the great weight of the evidence and either is a miscarriage of justice or cries out to be overturned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Third Circuit law (applied here), the new-trial inquiry asks whether the verdict is against the great weight of the evidence and whether overturning it is necessary to avoid a miscarriage of justice. The district court’s decision is reviewed for abuse of discretion. Cite: Vectura Ltd. v. GlaxoSmithKline LLC; Leonard v. Stemtech Int’l Inc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of appellate review for post-trial procedural rulings
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court’s procedural rulings are reviewed under the regional circuit’s law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing procedural rulings on appeal, the Federal Circuit applies the law of the relevant regional circuit. For example, here Third Circuit law governed review standards (abuse of discretion for new-trial denials). Cite: MLC Intell. Prop., LLC v. Micron Tech., Inc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for denial of JMOL (Rule 50)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Third Circuit reviews a district court’s denial of a motion for JMOL de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts review the legal sufficiency of the evidence supporting the jury verdict without deference to the district court’s conclusion when reviewing denials of JMOL. Cite: Pac. Biosciences; Pitts v. Delaware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 50(b) preservation requirement (must move under Rule 50(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Rule 50(b), a party must have first moved for JMOL under Rule 50(a) at the close of all the evidence in order to preserve the right to renew that same JMOL motion after the jury returns its verdict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to move under Rule 50(a) before close of evidence results in forfeiture of the right to bring a post-verdict Rule 50(b) JMOL. A party cannot rely on the opposing party’s Rule 50(a) motion or the district court’s denial of that motion to satisfy Rule 50(a)’s preservation requirement. Cite: Comaper Corp. v. Antec, Inc.; Kars 4 Kids Inc. v. American Can!

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture vs waiver in JMOL context
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party fails to make a Rule 50(a) motion before the close of evidence, it forfeits (forfeiture doctrine) its right to seek JMOL under Rule 50(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion distinguishes forfeiture from waiver and notes that failing to take the step of moving for JMOL results in forfeiture of the Rule 50(b) remedy. Courts will look for an actual Rule 50(a) motion to preserve rights. Cite: In re Google Tech. Holdings LLC (discussion of terminology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Rule of Evidence 403 balancing test for excluding evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court may exclude relevant evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by a danger of unfair prejudice, confusing the issues, misleading the jury, undue delay, wasting time, or needlessly presenting cumulative evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When excluding evidence (here, an unasserted patent) the court must weigh probative value against countervailing considerations. Potential downstream burdens (e.g., a 'mini-trial' to show whether an unasserted patent covers the accused product) support exclusion under Rule 403. Cite: Fed. R. Evid. 403; Acumed LLC v. Advanced Surgical Servs., Inc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluding evidence of unasserted patents when probative value is low
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court may exclude references to unasserted patents if admission would require collateral mini-trials or would add little probative value relative to confusion or waste of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that an unasserted patent 'shows the novel idea' for a component is insufficient if it would necessitate a separate trial on whether that patent covers the accused products; low probative value plus risk of mini-trial supports exclusion under Rule 403.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of noninfringement verdict on validity proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: When the jury finds that the accused products did not infringe the asserted claims, the jury need not return a verdict on the validity of the asserted claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trial court and verdict form can (and did) instruct the jury not to decide validity if it finds noninfringement as to the asserted claims. This conserves trial resources and follows standard practice when infringement is not found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court’s claim construction statements vs demonstratives/party arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: The district court’s formal claim construction is what the court announces and reads to the jury; demonstratives or slides prepared by parties reflecting the court’s rulings or additional 'no disclaimer' language are party arguments and are not the court’s construction unless adopted by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A demonstrative containing extra language (e.g., a 'no disclaimer' line) does not constitute a modification of the court’s construction. Parties may be permitted to argue the meaning of the construction (e.g., that it does not exclude gravity drop), but the court controls the formal construction given to the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim term development: court need not sua sponte construe terms not requested
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party never requests a construction of a particular claim term (here, 'capture'), the district court need not construe that term and the factual question of whether the accused device meets the term is for the jury to resolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should request construction of disputed claim terms during claim construction; otherwise, the jury decides application of the existing construction. The absence of a requested construction means the party cannot later complain that the court failed to construe that term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible scope of trial argumentation when claim construction language is excluded from jury instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the court declines to include certain explanatory or 'no disclaimer' language in the final jury instructions, parties may argue their interpretation of the court’s construction to the jury (so long as it does not contravene the court’s formal construction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may limit demonstratives or argument to avoid jury confusion, but they can allow parties to make arguments that the court’s construction permits (e.g., that the court’s construction does not exclude a gravity drop). Trial counsel should preserve arguments appropriately for appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of trial evidence (demos, videos, expert testimony) to prove mode of operation
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may rely on live demonstrations, slowed videos, expert testimony, and engineering testimony to show how an accused product operates (e.g., whether it captures seeds or projects/accelerates them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sufficiency and weight of such evidence is a factual question for the jury; appellate courts give deference to district court factfinding on new-trial motions (abuse-of-discretion) but review JMOL de novo. Demonstrative/experimental evidence may be persuasive to a jury on issues of operation and timing (e.g., seed acceleration metrics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate jurisdiction for patent appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Circuit has jurisdiction over appeals from district courts in patent cases under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should cite and rely on the Federal Circuit as the appellate forum for patent case appeals as provided by statute.
